regions.name: Frontal lobe
regions.summary: The front of the cerebral cortex, involved in planning, decision-making, voluntary movement and aspects of personality.
fields: Primary motor cortex, premotor cortex, prefrontal cortex, Broca's area (usually left hemisphere).
Executive function, working memory, movement initiation, speech production.
Frontal damage can alter planning, impulse control and social behaviour (famous case: Phineas Gage, 1848).

regions.name: Parietal lobe
regions.summary: Integrates sensory information about touch, body position and spatial relationships.
fields: Primary somatosensory cortex (postcentral gyrus), posterior parietal cortex.
Touch, proprioception, spatial attention, combining senses to guide action.
Right parietal damage can cause hemispatial neglect: ignoring one side of space.

regions.name: Temporal lobe
regions.summary: Processes hearing, language comprehension and plays a major part in memory.
fields: Primary auditory cortex, Wernicke's area (usually left), hippocampus and amygdala lie deep inside.
Auditory processing, understanding speech, recognising objects and faces, memory formation.
Temporal lobe epilepsy can produce unusual sensory experiences before a seizure.

regions.name: Occipital lobe
regions.summary: The visual processing centre at the back of the brain.
fields: Primary visual cortex (V1) and higher visual areas.
Edges, orientation, motion, colour and form processing. Information then flows to dorsal ('where/how') and ventral ('what') pathways.
Damage to V1 can cause blind regions in the visual field even when the eyes are healthy.

regions.name: Hippocampus
regions.summary: A seahorse-shaped structure in the medial temporal lobe, essential for forming new explicit memories and for spatial navigation.
fields: Consolidating episodic and semantic memories; place cells help map space.
One of the few regions where adult neurogenesis has been studied; its extent in adult humans is still debated.
Early Alzheimer's disease commonly affects hippocampal circuits.

regions.name: Amygdala
regions.summary: An almond-shaped cluster of nuclei that helps evaluate emotional significance, especially threat and fear.
fields: Emotional learning, fear conditioning, tagging memories with emotional salience.
It is part of wider circuits; it is not simply 'the fear centre'.
Links to hippocampus, prefrontal cortex and hypothalamus.

regions.name: Thalamus
regions.summary: A paired relay station deep in the brain that routes most sensory information to the cortex.
fields: Sensory relay (vision, hearing, touch), attention and sleep-wake regulation.
Smell (olfaction) reaches the cortex without first passing through the thalamus.
Thalamic stroke can cause sensory loss or altered consciousness.

regions.name: Cerebellum
regions.summary: The 'little brain' at the back of the skull. It holds a large fraction of the brain's neurons.
fields: Coordinating movement, balance, motor learning and timing. Also linked to some cognitive functions.
Cerebellar damage causes ataxia: unsteady, uncoordinated movement.

regions.name: Brainstem
regions.summary: Midbrain, pons and medulla: connects the brain to the spinal cord.
fields: Controls breathing, heart rate regulation, arousal and passes motor and sensory tracts.
Most cranial nerves emerge from the brainstem.
Because vital functions are concentrated here, small lesions can have severe effects.

neural_topics.name: The neuron
neural_topics.summary: The basic signalling cell of the nervous system.
fields: Dendrites receive input; the soma (cell body) integrates it; the axon carries output; axon terminals release neurotransmitter.
The human brain has roughly 86 billion neurons (estimate) plus a similar order of glial cells.

neural_topics.name: Dendrites
neural_topics.summary: Branched extensions that collect signals from other neurons.
fields: Many synapses form on small protrusions called dendritic spines, which can change shape during learning.
Dendrites do more than relay: they can perform local processing before signals reach the soma.

neural_topics.name: Axons and myelin
neural_topics.summary: The axon carries the action potential away from the cell body.
fields: Fatty insulation made by oligodendrocytes (CNS) or Schwann cells (PNS).
Myelin and nodes of Ranvier allow saltatory conduction, much faster than in unmyelinated axons.
Multiple sclerosis involves immune-mediated damage to CNS myelin.

neural_topics.name: Action potential
fields: Resting about -70 mV; depolarisation to threshold (about -55 mV) opens voltage-gated Na+ channels; Na+ rushes in; K+ channels open and K+ exits to repolarise; a brief hyperpolarisation follows.
Stronger stimuli produce more spikes per second, not bigger spikes.
Use the Neural Simulator to see a simplified model.

neural_topics.name: The synapse
neural_topics.summary: The junction where one neuron signals to another.
fields: An action potential opens Ca2+ channels; vesicles fuse and release neurotransmitter, which binds receptors on the next cell.
Gap junctions pass current directly, giving very fast, often synchronised signalling.
Transmitter is removed by reuptake, enzymatic breakdown or diffusion.

neural_topics.name: Neurotransmitters
fields: Main excitatory transmitter in the CNS.
Main inhibitory transmitter in the brain.
Involved in reward learning, motivation and movement. It is not simply 'the pleasure chemical'.
Modulates mood, sleep and appetite. Most of the body's serotonin is in the gut.

neural_topics.name: Excitation and inhibition
neural_topics.summary: Each neuron integrates thousands of inputs.
fields: Excitatory inputs push the membrane toward threshold; inhibitory inputs push it away.
Spatial and temporal summation determine whether the axon hillock reaches threshold and fires.
Healthy brain activity depends on a balance of excitation and inhibition.

memory_topics.name: Types of memory
fields: Hold a few items for seconds to a minute; working memory also manipulates them (prefrontal cortex).
Episodic (events) and semantic (facts); rely on the hippocampus and cortex.
Procedural skills, priming and conditioning; involve basal ganglia, cerebellum and other circuits.

memory_topics.name: Memory consolidation
memory_topics.summary: New memories are initially fragile and become stable over time.
fields: Synaptic consolidation happens within hours; systems consolidation gradually shifts storage from hippocampus to cortex.
Sleep, especially slow-wave and REM stages, supports consolidation. The precise mechanisms are an active research area.

memory_topics.name: Long-term potentiation
memory_topics.summary: A lasting strengthening of synapses after repeated activity.
fields: Strong stimulation activates NMDA receptors, Ca2+ enters the cell, and AMPA receptors are added to the synapse.
'Cells that fire together wire together' is a useful summary of Hebbian plasticity.
A leading cellular model of learning. Linking LTP directly to behaviour is still being refined.

memory_topics.name: Neuroplasticity
memory_topics.summary: The nervous system changes its structure and function with experience.
fields: Synaptic strengthening and weakening, new dendritic spines, rewiring after injury, and in some regions neurogenesis.
Some systems, such as vision, are especially plastic early in life.
'Brain training' claims often outrun the evidence.

memory_topics.name: Forgetting
memory_topics.summary: Forgetting is normal and can be adaptive.
fields: Decay of weak traces, interference from similar memories, and failure of retrieval cues.
His 1885 forgetting curve showed rapid early loss followed by slower decline.
Spreading study over time improves long-term retention.

memory_topics.name: Learning how to learn
memory_topics.summary: Evidence-based study strategies from cognitive science.
fields: Spread sessions out and mix related topics.
Explain ideas in your own words and connect them to what you know.
